newsitem.title: USA: Oversubscribed Mexico bond proves market liquidity.
newsitem.headline: Oversubscribed Mexico bond proves market liquidity.

text.p: To the relief of emerging market watchers, demand for Mexico's jumbo global bond showed the market is swimming in liquidity, experts said.
The bond is more than twice oversubscribed and of the 170 accounts participating, more than half were first-time buyers, said a syndicate source.
The 10-year global bond, with 9.875 percent coupon, is priced at par, yielding 335 basis points over U.S. Treasuries.
"This is the tightest spread for any UMS issuance," he said. Twenty- and 30-year bonds issued last year were priced at 445 basis points over, he added.
"The number of first-time buyers is encouraging," said Ingrid Iverson, emerging market fixed income strategist at UBS Securities. "It shows many cross-buyers are out there."

First-time buyers, as opposed to seasoned players, are more likely to hold on to the securities longer, thus giving the bond more price stability, she said. "They aren't likely to sell into the rally soon."

The closely watched deal, which had been expected to set the tone for emerging market sovereign new issues in 1997, was hailed as fairly priced and well-managed by co-leads Merrill Lynch and Salomon Brothers.
"It is not a give-away," said a trader, "but people seem to be happy."
Other Mexican global bonds traded on the secondary market gained about 1/2 point, outperforming the Latin dollar debt market, he said.
"The yield came below the interpolated curve," said Raul Elizalde, quantitative analyst of emerging market debt at ING Barings. "But it does not mean it can get cheaper."
The whole yield curve is expected to move lower to reflect Mexico's improving credit position, he said.
In this scenario, the 30-year global bond issued last year could tighten by 75 basis points in 1997, which would make a 50 basis point compression for this 10-year issue possible, he said.
The immediate after-market outlook, however, is less clear, becuase some buy would shy away from paying much above par for the freshly minted issues, Elizalde said.
The 10-year maturity fills an important gap on Mexico's dollar debt yield curve for estabilishing a liquid benchmark, he said, estimating that the bond has a duration of 6.2 years.
The popularity of this issue could potentially rob some luster out of the 20-year issue, he said.
Elizalde noted that the success of this Mexico deal bodes well for the coming $2 billion global bonds of Argentina.
"It is good for Argentina," he said. "It shows the market has good appetite for sovereign debt."
